newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Make drugs legal, EU Commissioner says.
newsitem.headline: Make drugs legal, EU Commissioner says.

text.p: Drugs should be legalised, European Commissioner Emma Bonino said on Thursday, because years of prohibition simply had not worked.

"Thanks to prohibitionist policies drugs are now goods whose production, trade and consumption are illegal as well as out of control. And yet they are probably the only goods which one can buy anytime and anywhere," she told an anti-prohibition rally.

"McDonalds outlets occasionally close. So do gas stations. But you will always be able to buy an illegal drug, no matter where you are and if it's Christmas Eve or Ramadan," she said, stressing that she was speaking personally and not for the Commission.
"...pedlars never stop: they have such fat margins that they just cannot afford to tire," she added.

The Italian Commissioner stressed that she was personally against drug use and did not take them herself, but their use was a matter of personal choice and she had not found any evidence over the past 20 years that prohibition worked.

"We have been experimenting with drug prohibition for several decades now and those are the results," she said, pointing to rises in the production, availability and use of illegal drugs and linked violence and exposure to AIDS.

Last week the Netherlands -- which allows the sale of small amounts of soft drugs in so-called "coffee shops" and turns a blind eye to possession of small amounts of hard drugs -- fought off pressure from the other 14 EU states to change its policy.

Dutch Socialist Euro-MP Hedy D'Ancona told Thursday's conference French President Jacques Chirac had led the move "for grandstanding reasons" to force the Hague to reverse a policy which had helped reduce addiction.

Bonino, who said cannabis had never killed anyone and "is the first that should be legalised", is the only member of the 20-member EU executive to have spoken out openly for the decriminalisation of drugs.

The EU's Justice Commissioner Anita Gradin has said in the past that advocating decriminalisation of drug abuse "makes no sense at all" and that the effects of liberalisation experiments were disastrous.
